teaser.text: Tesla is a company that sells electric cars and equipment that makes, stores, and moves electricity. Its business is easiest to understand by following a dollar from the customer, through the product and its costs, to the profit left over.

blocks.heading: Where could Tesla's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted price is $284.52 in October 2027, a 24% loss including dividends. It rises to $300.93 in October 2028, still a 20% loss. By October 2029, it reaches $336.44, a 10% loss.
The bear case has a 30% probability. The base case has a 55% probability. The bull case has a 15% probability. The October 2029 range runs from $63.43 to $971.74. Today's reference price is $375.00.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Tesla?

paragraphs.text: EBITDA rises from $17,500M in October 2027 to $25,000M in October 2029, with $21,000M in between. The path assumes vehicle recovery, continued storage growth and better fixed-cost absorption. Energy gross profit rose from $2,640M to $3,802M, but vehicle deliveries fell 8.6% in 2025 and automotive gross margin excluding credits stayed at 15.4%. The bear row falls from $12,500M to $10,000M before recovering to $11,000M, while the bull row rises from $20,000M to $35,000M as battery constraints ease and higher-margin software becomes material.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Tesla really make?

paragraphs.text: The weighted price is $284.52 in October 2027 and $336.44 in October 2029. That implies a 24% loss including dividends by October 2027 and a 10% loss by October 2029. The bear case is $63.43 and the base case is $312.09. The bull case is $971.74; the probabilities are 30% bear, 55% base and 15% bull. Tesla’s real free cash flow was 3.6% of revenue, while stock pay was $0.80 per share in 2025.

Stock compensation creates another gap. Tesla adds this noncash expense back because shares, rather than cash, go to employees. But shareholders still bear an economic cost through dilution. Deducting $2,825 million from reported free cash flow gives a stricter view, without making Tesla’s official measure mathematically wrong.

earnings.title: Tesla earnings date, guidance and results
earnings.meta_description: Tesla reports October 21, 2026; its guide is more than $25 billion of 2026 capex, with deliveries and cash the key test.
earnings.opening: Tesla plans to release Q3 results on October 21, 2026. Watch whether higher deliveries produce cash.
earnings.closing: The full memo answers how Tesla makes money, faces rivals, is managed and carries risks.

paragraphs.text: The current 2026 capex guide is more than $25 billion. The 2025 annual report had anticipated spending above $20 billion, so the programme expanded during the year. In Q2, operating cash flow was $4.697 billion. Capex was $5.789 billion, leaving negative free cash flow of $1.092 billion. Free cash flow therefore shows whether the business still has cash after operating costs and investment.

blocks.heading: Did Tesla keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Tesla certified all the milestones in Musk’s earlier award. But Musk forecast vehicle-sales growth of 20%–30% for 2025. Actual deliveries fell 8.6%. Earlier achievements deserve credit, while later promises still need to be tested against deadlines and commercial results.

blocks.heading: What are Tesla's revenue and profit trends?

paragraphs.text: Q2 2026 showed a sales recovery, not yet an earnings recovery. Revenue rose 25.5% year over year, and vehicle deliveries reached 480,126.

Gross margin slipped to 16.8%, while operating income fell to $398 million. Gross margin is the share of revenue left after direct costs; operating income also subtracts ongoing expenses. Tesla sold more while retaining less operating profit.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Tesla's next results?

paragraphs.text: Tesla plans to release Q3 results on October 21, 2026. It reported 486,532 deliveries for the quarter. Deliveries can spread factory costs across more vehicles, but only if prices and costs leave enough money on each sale. Annual deliveries fell from 1,789,226 in 2024 to 1,636,129 in 2025, so the new figure is a signal, not proof of improved revenue, profit or cash conversion.
